questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a building permits
questions.learningObjective: say what a theatre's architecture allows a production to do
questions.stem: A theatre's building is not a neutral container but a set of decisions about where an audience can see from and how far a voice has to carry. Which of these is something a building decides in advance of any play?

options.text: The relationship between the audience and the stage, since the seating, the walls, and the roof fix what can be seen and from where
The meaning the play will carry, since a building is built to express the intentions of the people who raised the money for it
options.misconception: credits architecture with a thesis, which is a claim about patronage and not about sightlines

options.text: The number of performances the company can give, since a building with more exits can be cleared faster between shows
options.misconception: promotes a practical convenience into the building's main function, which is what the audience is for

options.text: Which plays will suit the house, since a building acquires a character that its management is then obliged to respect
options.misconception: reverses the dependence, since a repertoire is chosen for a building and not the reverse

questions.explanation: The building is the first thing a production has to accept, because it fixes the terms on which everything after it happens. Where the seats are, how far the first row is from the stage, whether the roof can carry a gallery, whether the walls are plaster or brick, and how high the room is together determine what an actor can do with a face, a whisper, or a crowd, and they do it before anybody writes a line. That is the first option, and the three items in it are all architecture. The second makes a building an author, and patrons have expressed plenty of ambitions without the fabric recording them. The third picks one practical feature and calls it the function. The fourth inverts a real dependence, since a repertory company takes the shape of the house it plays, and the classics in a shallow building are a different repertory from the classics in a deep one.
questions.hint: Ask what is settled before a writer or a director arrives.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A thrust stage and its intimacy
questions.learningObjective: say what a thrust stage does to the relationship between actors and audience
questions.stem: In a thrust stage the audience sits on three sides of the playing area, which projects among them rather than behind a frame. What does that arrangement create?

options.text: A nearness with consequences, since three sides of the room must all be able to see and hear, which limits what a production can put on stage
A larger capacity, since a room open on three sides can be filled more cheaply than one closed at the front
options.misconception: claims a financial advantage, which is a question about costs and not about the audience's position

options.text: A neutral frame, since a play performed on a thrust is freed from the picture-frame convention and so has no front at all
options.misconception: supposes the absence of a frame removes every set of terms, when a thrust has its own and stricter ones

options.text: An audience that watches as a body, since three sides of people see the same action from differing angles and so share a single view
options.misconception: assumes a shared angle, when the three sides see the stage from opposed directions

questions.explanation: The intimacy on a thrust is not free, and the price is written into the arrangement. If the audience is on three sides then three sides of the room must have a usable view, so nothing can be built for one audience that blinds another, a performer has to turn rather than project, and the biggest effects in a repertory are frequently impossible for a season. That is the first option, and its second clause is the part that distinguishes the arrangement from a description of it. The second is a claim about construction costs and says nothing about what the audience experiences. The third removes a convention and concludes that no terms remain, which is the opposite of the case, since a thrust imposes its own discipline on everything from entrances to levels. The fourth assumes the three sides see alike, and they see in opposed directions, which is the central technical problem of the form.
questions.hint: Ask what the three sides of the audience must each be able to see.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A proscenium and the picture it enforces
questions.learningObjective: say what a proscenium arch does to the audience's expectations
questions.stem: A proscenium arch separates the stage from the auditorium with a frame, so the audience looks at the stage as at a picture. What does that frame establish?

options.text: A convention about where reality stops, since everything inside the frame belongs to the play and everything outside belongs to the room
A guarantee of good sightlines, since a fixed opening can be measured so that every seat has an equal view of the whole stage
options.misconception: assumes the frame solves what it frames, since a wide arch is exactly what makes sightlines difficult

options.text: A way of admitting more people, since a seated house with a single front can be raked more steeply than one open at the sides
options.misconception: makes an architectural form do the work of an engineering decision about sightlines

options.text: A licence for the audience to move, since a framed picture invites viewers to step back and consider it as an object
options.misconception: credits a frame with mobility, when the audience is seated in rows and cannot step back at all

questions.explanation: The arch draws a line and everything depends on where the line falls. A set that crosses it is a piece of the world; the same object carried through the auditorium is a piece of stage carpentry, and the convention has to be held consistently or the audience loses its footing. That is the first option, and the second clause is what the frame is for: it tells the audience which reality they are watching. The second is a non sequitur, since a wide opening is harder to see past than a narrow one. The third is an argument about raking and belongs to the auditorium, not to the arch. The fourth gives the audience a freedom it does not have, since a seated house cannot step back, and the frame invites a kind of attention rather than a change of place.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a set that crosses the frame.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An open stage and its sightlines
questions.learningObjective: say what an open stage has to solve that a framed stage does not
questions.stem: An open stage is a bare platform with no scenery, so the room around it is used as the setting rather than painted in. What has such a production to do that a scenic one does not?

options.text: Keep every position readable from every seat, since there is no set to carry the eye and the arrangement has to do that work instead
Build a larger stage, since a bare platform cannot hold a crowd scene and the actors must have room to move in it
options.misconception: answers an aesthetic problem with floor space, when the difficulty is what can be seen from where

options.text: Cut the music, since a bare stage leaves the audience with nothing between it and the voices in the room
options.misconception: supplies a rule the form does not impose, since sound is available to any production that wants it

options.text: Use the house lights, since an unlit room would leave the audience looking at a platform it can barely see
options.misconception: prescribes a lighting state when the design of the light is one of the choices being made

questions.explanation: Scenery is normally a device for telling an audience where to look, and an open stage takes that device away, so the production has to supply the function some other way. Figures have to be placed so that the composition holds from the far side of the house as well as the near, entrances have to be chosen to keep a sightline open, and a crowd has to be distributed rather than merely assembled. That is the first option, and the clause about the arrangement doing the work a set would have done is the point. The second answers a problem of legibility with a problem of area, and more floor space makes an unreadable arrangement larger. The third and fourth both prescribe a single technical choice, and both of those choices are among the things an open stage leaves open rather than settles.
questions.hint: Ask what scenery was doing for the audience that this production must now do itself.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A touring company and its constraint
questions.learningObjective: state the constraint a touring company works under
questions.stem: A touring company performs the same production in a run of towns, playing whatever halls it is given. Which constraint follows from the arrangement itself?

options.text: The scenery and the staging have to travel, so whatever the company can carry becomes the limit on what the production may contain
The company must be large, since a small group cannot cover a run of dates and so the repertoire has to be broad
options.misconception: assumes size is forced, when a small touring company can and does work with a narrow repertoire

options.text: The audiences are strangers, so a touring production must explain itself more plainly than one in a home city
options.misconception: moves the constraint to reception, when what travelling settles is what the production can physically be

options.text: The company must own its scenery outright, since hired equipment cannot be relied on to arrive with the players
options.misconception: asserts a financial rule, which is a matter of arrangements and not of the touring condition itself

questions.explanation: Touring is a transport problem, and the transport problem is the artistic one. Everything in the production has to be carried by a lorry, unloaded, and set up in a room nobody in the company has seen, usually in a few hours, by a crew who are also packing. Every big effect in the repertory is therefore unavailable unless it happens to fold, and the shape of the company's work is decided by what its van will hold. That is the first option, and the last clause is why the constraint reaches into the playwright's choice of material. The second confuses a practical arrangement with a condition, since small touring companies are common and their repertoire is narrow by design. The third relocates the difficulty to the audience. The fourth states a financial practice, and a practice is not what follows from the arrangement itself.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be carried, and who has to put it up.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A repertory company and its ensemble
questions.learningObjective: state what a repertory company's fixed ensemble provides
questions.stem: A repertory company keeps the same actors and plays a changing list, so that a production in March and one in November share a cast. What does that arrangement give the work?

options.text: A set of comparisons the audience can make, since having seen an actor play one part can change what is heard in another
A guaranteed income for the actors, since a fixed company can plan a season and a visiting player cannot
options.misconception: confuses the arrangement with a contract, since nothing in a repertory fixes anybody's pay

options.text: A smaller repertoire, since a company that keeps the same actors must choose the plays that suit them best
options.misconception: confuses a company with its casting, since the same actors can appear in anything the company acquires

options.text: A shorter rehearsal period, since a permanent company has already worked out how it will do a scene like this one before
options.misconception: supplies a working assumption about efficiency, which is a matter of a production and not of the season

questions.explanation: A repertory company is a set of comparisons in the audience's head, and that is its principal effect on the work. Somebody who saw a young actor be flippant in a comedy in March is watching a murderer in November, and the two are present at once, which is not available to a production assembled fresh from strangers or to a play read in a book. It also means a production can be built on what the company already does well, and a director can assume a shared shorthand. That is the first option, and the last clause is the mechanism. The second turns an arrangement into a contract, which is a separate matter of employment. The third confuses the company's continuity with its casting, and the same actors appear in whatever the company acquires. The fourth imports an assumption about rehearsal, which is a decision taken per production.
questions.hint: Ask what an audience brings into the theatre from the previous production.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A licensing system and what it censors
questions.learningObjective: state what a licensing system actually controls
questions.stem: For centuries in England a play could not be performed without a licence from an office that examined the text, and one part of that examination was what the play implied rather than what it said. What did the system control?

options.text: The political meaning of a play, since a text could be refused for what an audience might reasonably take from it
The truth of a play, since a text was examined for whether its history was reported accurately before it was staged
options.misconception: confuses censorship with a historical accuracy office, which is not what the examiners were doing

options.text: The rights of the playwright, since a licence established who owned a text and could therefore be performed
options.misconception: conflates a censorship function with copyright, which is a separate arrangement entirely

options.text: The number of performances, since a licence was granted for a fixed number of nights and could not be extended
options.misconception: gives the system a scheduling function it did not have, since the licence covered the play and not its run

questions.explanation: The examinor's question was what a play would do to an audience, not what it said on the page, and that is what makes the system a censorship rather than a correction. A text could pass every test for decency and still be refused for putting a king's subjects on a stage looking at a king, because the implication was the offence and the implication was the thing the audience supplied. That is the first option, and its second clause is the whole mechanism. The second confuses the office with an accuracy check, which was never its function. The third imports copyright, which is a different legal arrangement and has nothing to do with the examination. The fourth makes the licence a permit for a run, and the thing it permitted was the performance of the play.
questions.hint: Ask whether the examiners judged the words or what the words would let an audience think.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a dramaturg does
questions.learningObjective: state the dramaturg's actual function in a production
questions.stem: A dramaturg is a role in a theatre, more used in continental practice than in the commercial theatre. What is the job?

options.text: To hold the text in view, so the director is asked what the play is doing and what in it is being missed
To keep the rehearsal on schedule, since the person with the plan must hold the company to the time available
options.misconception: confuses the dramaturg with the stage manager, whose authority is over the schedule and the running of the show

options.text: To write the scenes the playwright did not finish, since a production is entitled to supply what a text leaves out
options.misconception: credits the role with authorship, which would make the dramaturg a collaborator on the words

options.text: To find the contemporary parallels, since a director should be shown the world the play is about rather than the one it was written in
options.misconception: makes a research task the role's purpose, which is one thing such a person may do and not the office

questions.explanation: The dramaturg is the person who speaks for the play in a rehearsal room, which means the text, and the work is to keep the production in contact with it. When a staging begins to drift into the private taste of a director or a designer, somebody has to be able to say that the play is doing something else and that the room has stopped noticing what it is doing. That is the first option, and the phrase about what is being missed is the second half of the role. The second describes the stage manager, who is a different office with different authority and is addressed on the night. The third makes the dramaturg a writer of scenes, which would be a collaboration on the text. The fourth reduces the role to research, which is useful work and not the position.
questions.hint: Ask who in the room is responsible for saying what the play is doing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A concept statement and what it commits to
questions.learningObjective: say what a director's concept statement commits a production to
questions.stem: A director writes a concept statement before rehearsals, in which a single proposition about the play is set out and the design is argued from it. What does the statement commit the production to?

options.text: To a reading it can be held to, since once the proposition is written every staging decision can be tested against it in the room
To the playwright's intention, since a concept that departs from what the author meant cannot be defended to anybody
options.misconception: makes the author's intention a legal test, which no production is subject to and every production disputes

options.text: To a unified design, since a production with a single proposition must therefore have a single colour, a single period, and a single idea
options.misconception: takes a unity of purpose to require a unity of everything else, which is not what the statement governs

options.text: To the audience's expectations, since a proposition stated in advance becomes a promise the company must keep whatever happens on the night
options.misconception: treats the statement as a public contract, when it is an instrument used inside the company

questions.explanation: The value of writing the proposition down is that it becomes testable. Once a director has said in a document that the play is about a debt that is never acknowledged, then a designer who brings in a comic forest and an actor who plays the father as a villain are not simply disagreeing about taste, they are departing from something the room agreed to and can be asked about it in those terms. The statement is an instrument for the company, and its first use is internal. That is the first option, and the last clause is what makes it an instrument rather than a decoration. The second makes the author's intention a test that binds, and production history is largely the history of disagreeing with it. The third confuses unity of purpose with uniformity of design, and a single proposition is compatible with strong contrasts. The fourth makes a planning document a public promise, and the audience is not in the room when it is written.
questions.hint: Ask what the statement lets a rehearsal room say to a designer.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A design element and the meaning it carries
questions.learningObjective: say how a design element carries meaning in a production
questions.stem: A production fills a bare stage with a single long table, and the table is used for a wedding feast, a debt negotiation, and a death. What makes the object carry that range of meaning?

options.text: The recurrence, since an object that returns in three kinds of scene accumulates what each of them meant and can be read as all three at once
Its size, since a large object in an empty room is read as important and a small one is read as incidental
options.misconception: fixes the meaning in a property of the object, when the same table can be staged to mean opposite things

options.text: The budget spent on it, since an audience reads the cost of an object as a statement about the value of the household that owns it
options.misconception: moves the meaning to the production ledger, which is a real constraint and not a semiotic one

options.text: The period of the object, since a heavy oak table places a scene in a century and the rest follows from where it has put the audience
options.misconception: makes period the carrier, when a period is one thing an object can do among several

questions.explanation: An object on a stage is not a symbol until it is used more than once, and the accumulation is the mechanism. The table is a table at the wedding and a table at the deathbed, and by the third use the audience is reading all of it, so the object has become a compressed account of what the household does at its turning points. That is the first option, and the clause about being read as all three at once is the effect. The second fixes the meaning in the object's dimensions, which is a real constraint on how it can be staged and not a reading. The third confuses what an object costs with what it means, though spending does tell an audience something. The fourth makes period the carrier, and a period is one of several things an object can be doing.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the object appears and what it has collected by the last time.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Costume as a period signal
questions.learningObjective: say what costume tells an audience before anybody speaks
questions.stem: A production sets a play in a port city and dresses its cast in the working clothes of a particular trade and decade. What is costume doing that the text alone could not do?

options.text: Locating the action in a trade and a decade, so the audience knows what kind of life is being reported and in what period
Telling the audience which characters matter, since a costume that looks worn cannot belong to somebody who is doing well
options.misconception: makes condition the signal, which is one thing a costume can say and not the one being asked about

options.text: Replacing the need for a set, since a room can be described by what its occupants are wearing and a bare stage needs no scenery
options.misconception: makes costume a substitute for design, which is a use made of it and not its defining work

options.text: Identifying the rank of each speaker, since a play's lines are ambiguous about class and the clothes have to settle it
options.misconception: makes costume the arbiter of a fact the text usually states, and which it states better than a wardrobe can

questions.explanation: Costume is the fastest information a production can deliver, because it arrives before the first line and is read at a glance. A trade and a decade in a working costume tell an audience that the play is about this kind of labour in this period, and everything the text then says is heard against that frame rather than in a vacuum. That is the first option, and the first clause is what makes the rest of it possible. The second notes a real effect, and worn clothing does carry a condition, but the question is about the signal the production is deliberately placing. The third treats costume as a set substitute, which is a legitimate use and not what the clothes are for. The fourth makes the wardrobe the authority on class, where the play's own text is the better evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience knows in the first ten seconds that the first speech would take a scene to establish.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A stage property and its realism
questions.learningObjective: say what a stage property is judged on
questions.stem: A property is anything the actors handle: a cup, a letter, a sword. By what standard is a property's realism judged on a stage?

options.text: By whether it behaves as the real object would in the actor's hands, since a paper cup used as a drinking vessel gives itself away
By how closely it matches the original, since an audience compares an object against what it knows that object to be
options.misconception: makes resemblance the standard, when what the audience tests under pressure is weight, sound, and breakage

options.text: By how old it looks, since a play set in a past century cannot be served by a prop that reads as new
options.misconception: takes patina as the whole test, since a new-looking object can be made to read as old very cheaply

options.text: By whether the audience can see it, since a property that is handled in shadow has failed whatever it is made of
options.misconception: reduces the question to visibility, when most properties are used precisely in scenes that are hard to light

questions.explanation: An actor handles a property, and the handling is the test. A real cup is heavy in a particular way, tips in a particular way, breaks if it is dropped, and makes a particular sound; an audience notices these things without knowing it is noticing, and the failure is nearly always a mismatch between the object and the effort. A plastic cup that rings like a bell when set down, or a sword that has no weight in a swing, ends the fiction for the length of a second. That is the first option, and the phrase about the actor's hands is the whole of it. The second makes resemblance the standard, which would make the question a matter of copying rather than of use. The third reduces realism to patina, which is one cheap axis and not the whole. The fourth makes visibility the criterion, and most properties are used in the least visible moments of a play.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the actor puts it down.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A lighting cue and what it withholds
questions.learningObjective: state what a lighting cue can control by way of information
questions.stem: A lighting cue is a numbered instruction to change the state of the lighting at a given point. Which of these is something a cue can do that a stage direction cannot?

options.text: Decide what the audience is not to attend to, since an area of the stage can be kept dark and so removed from attention without being removed from the room
Report the weather, since a light state can suggest a sky that no character has mentioned aloud
options.misconception: gives a cue a descriptive function it shares with a stage direction, which can do the same thing

options.text: Introduce a character, since a follow spot can single out one figure and announce an entrance without a sound
options.misconception: describes what a direction can equally do by naming the entrance and who it is

options.text: Say what a character is thinking, since a light that rises on a face at the right moment is a direct statement about that face
options.misconception: credits light with interior access, which it can support but never supplies on its own

questions.explanation: A stage direction can describe what the light is, and a cue can operate on attention, which is a different order of thing. Because light is selective, a production can leave a table lit at the edge of the stage and never bring the audience's attention to it, or bring it up in full during a scene in which nobody mentions it, and the audience has received something they cannot easily account for. That asymmetry between what is in the room and what is in the view is the cue's real power, and no direction can produce it by describing. That is the first option, and the last clause is the mechanism. The second, the third, and the fourth each give the cue something a direction or the actors can do, and a light state is a support for attention rather than a substitute for it.
questions.hint: Ask what a light can leave in the room but out of the view.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A sound cue and the transition it marks
questions.learningObjective: say what a sound cue does at the point where it comes
questions.stem: A sound cue is a numbered instruction to begin a sound at a point in the running order. What is a sound cue uniquely positioned to mark?

options.text: A transition the audience can hear happening, since a sound can begin before a change is visible and carry the audience across it
A transition the audience cannot see coming, since sound arrives in advance of the picture and so prepares the eye for what follows
options.misconception: keeps the sound in sequence after the change, which is the commonest case and not the one the cue enables

options.text: A transition that no direction has announced, since a cue is given to the operator and not to the company
options.misconception: confuses who receives an instruction with what the audience is given, since a sound is heard by both

options.text: A transition between two companies playing on the same stage, since only a sound can be heard from both sides at once
options.misconception: assumes two companies on one stage, which is a special arrangement and not the general case

questions.explanation: A sound can arrive at a moment when nothing visible has changed, and it can keep arriving while the change happens, which means the audience experiences the transition as continuous rather than as a cut. A carriage that is heard approaching and then heard stopping carries an audience from one time to another without a blackout and without a pause in the playing, and nothing else on a stage does that as economically. That is the first option, and the second clause is the part that distinguishes it from the common case. The second has the sequence wrong, since the cue usually follows the change and marks it rather than warning of it. The third confuses the audience for the crew, and a sound is heard by everybody in the building. The fourth invents a special arrangement to give the cue a job, and the job does not need it.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience hears while the visible change is still happening.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A stage manager's authority
questions.learningObjective: say what authority the stage manager carries on the night
questions.stem: The stage manager is the one person in a theatre whose job covers the running of the show itself. What does that job give the person?

options.text: The final say on whether a performance goes ahead, since nothing proceeds without the running order and the running order is the manager's
The authority to change the director's staging, since a cue cannot be cued without somebody's permission and the permission is the manager's to give
options.misconception: confuses the running order with the staging, which is the director's to change and the manager's to notice

options.text: The right to speak to the company as the playwright's representative, since the manager holds the text on the company's behalf
options.misconception: gives the manager a critical office, which belongs to the dramaturg and to the director

options.text: The last word on the design, since a set that cannot be moved in time has to be somebody's decision to abandon
options.misconception: assumes a design decision on the night, where a designer is present and the manager reports the delay

questions.explanation: The authority is procedural and it is absolute, because the running order is the document that decides when everything happens and no part of the show happens outside it. A performance can be delayed, stopped, resumed, or abandoned by the person holding that document, and that is a real power, exercised for technical reasons and occasionally for ones that are not. That is the first option, and the second clause is why the power cannot be argued with in the moment. The second confuses the running of the show with its staging, and a stage manager reports a change rather than making one. The third makes the manager a critic of the text, which is another office. The fourth assumes the manager can abandon a design, and the authority there belongs to the designer who has to live with the result.
questions.hint: Ask which document decides when every other thing happens.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The criteria in a review
questions.learningObjective: say what a critic's review measures
questions.stem: A notice in a newspaper reports that a production opened last week and was well received. What is such a notice principally a record of?

options.text: One spectator's account of how the evening went, given against stated criteria and addressed to people deciding whether to go
The standing of the production among others, since a notice is a placing in a field and the placing is the content
options.misconception: makes a notice a ranking exercise, which is one thing a notice may do and not what it is

options.text: The state of the art at that date, since a notice is evidence of what a moment's audiences were able to see
options.misconception: promotes a single evening to a claim about a period, which is a generalisation the notice cannot support

options.text: The terms on which the company has sold the production, since a notice advertises what has been paid for
options.misconception: mistakes a notice for an advertisement, and the two are written to be read in opposite frames

questions.explanation: A notice is one person's evening reported in print, and the two things that make it what it is are the criteria and the readership. It says what it thought the production was trying to do, whether it achieved it, and it is read by people who have not gone and are deciding whether to. That makes it an account with a position in it rather than a verdict, and a reader who has seen the production can disagree with both the account and the criteria. That is the first option, and its three clauses are the parts that matter. The second reduces the notice to a placing, which is one move a critic can make and not the form. Given a qualified endorsement, since a critic who finds a fault in a production cannot also find something in it worth having

The reports record the production, since an opening night is the only night on which the whole company is freshest

options.text: The season was badly timed, so the production was good and the calendar was bad and no inference follows about the work
options.misconception: excuses the result by an external cause, when the question is how two measures of one production can diverge

questions.learningObjective: state the economics behind a long run

The play is the only thing in the building, since a repertory cannot sustain an audience on a single production
options.misconception: asserts a company policy, when a single long run is one common way of covering a hall's costs

options.text: The company is not being paid, since a run that long would have been offered to another theatre by now
options.misconception: assumes mobility, which depends on contracts and on a company choosing to move

options.text: The production has stopped changing, since a long run cannot absorb new work without losing the audience it has built
options.misconception: treats immobility as the condition of a run, which is a habit of some managements and not a law

questions.explanation: A long run is an economic arrangement before it is a critical fact, and the arithmetic is unforgiving. questions.topic: Why a theatre remounts a work
questions.learningObjective: state what a repertory revival is for

The saving of a development cost, since a known play is easier to sell and does not need the advertising a new one does
options.misconception: makes a marketing economy the purpose, which is a reason and not what the practice is for

options.text: The preservation of the original staging, so the theatre can show what the earlier production looked like to those who were not there
options.misconception: assumes a revival is a reconstruction, and a new cast in a new staging shows the opposite habit

options.text: The use of a set already built, since the cost of scenery is the largest item in a production and can be amortised over two runs
options.misconception: confuses a financial motive with the artistic one, and most revivals rebuild anyway

questions.explanation: A revival is a second reading, and the whole point is that the first one is finished and unavailable. A play the audience knows well can be staged for what it did not do the first time, and a company that has lived with a text for years can find a reading that a first production had no time for; the audience's familiarity becomes an instrument rather than a hindrance. questions.topic: What a performance tradition fixes
questions.learningObjective: say what a performance tradition settles for a later production
questions.stem: A performance tradition is a settled way of staging a kind of play, passed on and adopted by companies that did not invent it. What does a tradition fix for those who take it up?

The correct performance, since a tradition carries within it the answer to how a work was meant to be done
options.misconception: turns a convention into a standard of correctness, which is the belief tradition is often wrongly accused of

options.misconception: assumes traditions travel with performers, when they travel through texts, training, and institutions

options.text: The audience's understanding of the text, since a settled form teaches the audience what the play is about before it starts
options.misconception: gives the tradition an explanatory function, which belongs to an introduction and not to a staging habit

questions.explanation: A tradition is a set of expectations that has hardened, and its value is that it makes a departure legible. When a kind of play has been given a form for fifty years, a production that breaks that form is not merely being different; it is making an argument that an audience can read against the norm, and an argument that would be impossible if the norm did not exist. The second makes the tradition a standard of correctness, and no tradition is that, though every tradition is accused of it. The third assumes practices travel with performers, and they travel with texts and institutions as much as with people. It has been replaced, since an audience buying a name is no longer buying a play and the text has nothing left to do
options.misconception: replaces rather than subordinates, which overstates the case and loses the interaction the question is about

options.text: It has been shortened, since a star production runs fewer performances and so has less time for the longer scenes
options.misconception: confuses a number of performances with a length of text, which are unrelated quantities

The text is not gone; it is subordinated, and the subordination is legible in the fact that critics are discussing a person when they have gone to discuss a work. That is the first option, and the reciprocity in the last clause is what makes it a relationship rather than a swamping. questions.topic: Documentary theatre and its source
questions.learningObjective: say what documentary theatre takes as its material
questions.stem: Documentary theatre builds its performance out of material drawn from real events: transcripts, records, testimony. What does that source do to the resulting piece?

options.text: It fixes a claim the piece is arguing about, since the records it uses are the ground the performance stands on and cannot be adjusted to the argument
It makes the piece unarguable, since a document is a fact and a fact cannot be disputed by an audience
options.misconception: guarantees truth in a source, and a transcript is evidence of what was said rather than of what happened

options.text: It guarantees the piece cannot be acted, since real people are being represented and a performance is a kind of fiction
options.misconception: assumes a rule about representation that the form exists to break, and it has broken it repeatedly

options.text: It fixes the running time, since a documentary is as long as the events it records and cannot be cut without losing the record
options.misconception: makes a source a schedule, and a documentary is edited like any other material

questions.explanation: The source is a constraint, and it is a constraint in a particular direction. Because the performance is standing on documents, the material has to be presented as the material it is, and a piece that wants a fact the records do not support has to argue rather than assert, which is the pressure that makes such work worth watching. That is the first option, and the last clause is the mechanism. The second mistakes a source for proof, and a transcript is a record of what was said rather than of what was the case. The third asserts a rule that the form has spent forty years breaking, and the fact that it has broken it is the interesting part. The fourth turns a source into a schedule, and documentary material is edited as heavily as anything else.

questions.topic: Site-specific work and its dependence on place
questions.learningObjective: say what a site-specific piece depends on
questions.stem: A site-specific piece is written for one place and is performed there, sometimes once. What is the practical consequence of that arrangement?

options.text: The work cannot be separated from the place, so a copy of it elsewhere would be a different work rather than the same one moved
The work cannot be revised, since a piece made for a single audience has nothing else to be revised for
options.misconception: asserts a rigidity the form does not impose, since a site piece can be revised for its own site

options.text: The work is not a performance at all, since a piece that happens once in a building is closer to an event than to a show
options.misconception: dismisses a category difference as though it removed the performance, which it does not

options.text: The work depends on the weather, since a piece performed outdoors is subject to conditions the building would have removed
options.misconception: assumes the site is outdoors, which is one common case and not the condition of the form

That is the first option, and the second clause is the precise thing at issue. The second asserts a rigidity the form does not have, since a site piece can be revised for its own site and often is. questions.topic: A devised piece and how it is written
questions.learningObjective: state how a devised piece is authored
questions.stem: A devised piece is made by a company through a process of work rather than written by one person beforehand. What follows from that?

There is no text to criticise, since a piece without a written script cannot be judged against what it intended to be about
options.misconception: supplies a criterion of judgement, and a devised piece can be judged against what the process was trying to find

options.text: The piece belongs to whoever improvised the best scene, since authorship in a devised work follows whoever supplied the material
options.misconception: makes authorship a matter of quantity supplied, when a devised text is assembled by a group decision

A play of whispers, since eighty feet is a long way for the voice and a balcony that far back will lose a quiet line

Keeping the cost down, since a single pattern of joinery is cheaper to buy and simpler to maintain than anything varied

A brighter account of the theft, since a single lamp is a convention for lighting an examination and the audience can now see the page

Warning of the change, since a sound that arrives before the picture moves gives the audience several seconds to prepare for the new state
options.misconception: keeps the sound before the fade, where the sheet places the fade as already under way when the bell sounds

options.text: Evidence of the distance between the two states, since a bell struck once and heard faintly places one of them in a village the other is not in
options.misconception: reads a geographic claim, where the sheet gives the bell as an effect rather than as a location

options.text: Notice of a scene change to the front of house, since a sound cue is also what tells the front of house manager that a scene is ending
options.misconception: gives a front of house function to a cue, and the manager is called on the running order rather than on a sound

questions.explanation: The sheet's detail is the overlap: the bell is struck on the last line, and the fade begins during it, and both states are lit at once for four seconds. questions.topic: The criteria behind a notice
questions.learningObjective: recover the criteria behind a described notice
questions.stem: A notice reads: the play is difficult and took some finding, and this production has not made that easier, but it has made it clear, so that the difficulty now belongs to the play's argument rather than to the evening's staging. Which criteria is the critic applying?

options.text: Whether the production's clarity is in the play's favour, so the test is what the staging does to the text rather than whether the text was easy
Whether the evening was enjoyable, so a critic who calls an evening difficult has failed the only test that matters at the box office
options.misconception: moves the criterion to pleasure, which the notice has explicitly set aside in favour of a distinction

options.text: Whether the casting suited the play, since a notice that mentions difficulty is usually also judging the company
options.misconception: supplies a casting test the notice never mentions, and the text of it names the staging only

options.text: Whether the production was original, since a staging that made a hard play clear has departed from what is usual
options.misconception: reads clarity as novelty, which is a different judgment about a different thing

It concedes that the play is difficult, refuses to blame the production for the difficulty, credits the production for removing a different kind of obstacle, and then makes its test explicit by asking where the difficulty now sits. The criterion is the text's position relative to the staging, and a reader who went can check every part of that, including whether the clarity was purchased at the cost of the play's problems. That is the first option, and the last clause is the sentence the critic has just written. The second substitutes enjoyment, which the notice sets aside. The third supplies a casting judgement the notice never makes. The fourth confuses clarity with novelty.
questions.hint: Ask what the critic says the difficulty now belongs to.

questions.topic: A verdict separated from its reasoning
questions.learningObjective: separate a verdict from the argument beneath it
questions.stem: A notice reads: the acting is beautiful and the play is not worth the evening, and one may reasonably ask whether the theatre has mistaken the two. What has this critic separated?

options.text: The two things the notice contains, since the quality of the performance and the worth of the work are being reported as independent findings and are open to separate disagreement
The company from the critic, since a notice that says the play was not worth it is really a comment on the critic's own taste

options.text: The audience from the notice, since a reader who disagrees has been told to look elsewhere for a verdict on the play
options.misconception: reads an instruction to the reader as a refusal to judge, and the critic has judged twice over

options.text: Nothing at all, since a notice that praises and blames the same production has cancelled itself out
options.misconception: assumes a mixed verdict is self-cancelling, when it can report two independent findings

Somebody who thought the production deserved the evening can accept the second finding and reject the first; somebody who found the acting extraordinary and the play worthless is in exactly the position the sentence describes, and that position is not a contradiction because the two claims are about different objects. A critic who had blurred them would have produced a notice nobody could use. That is the first option, and the last clause is the point. The second turns a critical claim into a preference and is defeated by the invitation to disagree. The third reads the invitation as a dismissal. The fourth assumes that praise and blame cancel, and they do not.

questions.topic: A convention the audience has stopped seeing
questions.learningObjective: identify evidence of a convention becoming invisible
questions.stem: A review of a revival of a familiar play notes that the production has made the audience forget that the play is two hundred years old: nobody coughs, and the young actors play their ages rather than their period. Which observation shows the convention losing its power?

options.text: The two hundred years, since an audience that has stopped noticing the age of the material is no longer registering the form as historical at all
The coughing, since a silent house is the measure of how completely a production has captured its audience
options.misconception: reads an auditorium habit as evidence about a convention, which is about how the material is being received

options.text: The young actors, since casting against type is the usual sign that a production has noticed what it is doing
options.misconception: makes casting the test, and casting is a choice rather than a report of what an audience has stopped seeing

options.text: The revival, since any return to an old play is itself a sign that its conventions have stopped working
options.misconception: makes revivals the evidence, and a revival usually revives the conventions it inherits

A play is a historical artefact and the audience knows it, and the moment a production makes them forget the date is the moment the forms belonging to that date stop being read as forms and start being read as behaviour, which is exactly what a convention has to do to become transparent. The review's phrase about playing ages rather than period is the same fact said twice. That is the first option, and the last clause is the mechanism. The second reads an auditorium habit, which is not evidence about a convention. The third makes the casting the test rather than a report. The fourth assumes revivals revive the conventions, which is what most of them do.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience has stopped registering.

questions.learningObjective: find the production record that defeats a general claim

Defeats both halves, since a company paying a woman is a company that employed women and the refused applicant was employed in effect
options.misconception: collapses an applicant into an employee, which is the difference the refusal in the claim turns on

options.text: Leaves the claim standing, since a paybook records money and the claim is about appearances on a stage
options.misconception: severs payment from appearance without reason, since payment for performances is the ordinary evidence of both

options.text: Leaves the claim standing, since one paybook cannot outweigh a history built on many documents of several kinds
options.misconception: asks a single record to outweigh a general claim, when a counter-example is enough and the record is the best kind

The second collapses an applicant into an employee and so destroys the distinction the refusal rests on. The third and fourth both try to protect the claim, and the third severs payment from appearance when a paybook for performances is the ordinary evidence of both, while the fourth asks one document to outweigh a general claim, which a counter-example never has to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a concept statement argues
questions.learningObjective: say what a concept statement asserts and how it constrains
questions.stem: A concept statement for an invented play reads: this is a play about two sisters who have agreed never to discuss their father's last year, and the last year has been performed twice on stage in identical detail, once by each sister, and in each version a different person is at fault. What is the statement asserting, and what does it oblige the production to do?

options.text: That the play's subject is an agreement rather than a fact, so the two versions must be given equal weight and neither may be settled as the true one
That the second version is the correction of the first, so the production must make the later account the one the audience is invited to accept
options.misconception: makes one version the verdict, and the statement's construction with two identical versions blocks that reading

options.text: That the father's year is a piece of history, so the production must research it accurately before it may be staged at all
options.misconception: insists on historical research the statement nowhere mentions and the doubling makes irrelevant

options.text: That the sisters are unreliable, so the production must show the audience which of the two accounts it prefers
options.misconception: draws a conclusion about the sisters' honesty that the statement has deliberately left open

questions.explanation: The statement locates the play's subject in an agreement rather than in a disputed fact, and everything else follows from that. The father's year is not something the production has to establish, because the play has arranged for it to be given twice in identical detail with the fault in a different place each time, and the symmetry is the argument: if the material is identical and the verdict is not, the verdict belongs to the teller. So the production is obliged to preserve the equality, to give both versions the same theatrical weight, and not to supply a device that would let the audience settle the question. That is the first option, and both clauses are load-bearing. The second makes the second version a correction, which the construction forbids. The third demands historical research the statement does not ask for. The fourth draws a conclusion about honesty the statement has carefully left open.
questions.hint: Ask what the doubling of the same detail with a different culprit is designed to prevent.

questions.topic: What a notice holds against a work
questions.learningObjective: say what a described notice measures
questions.stem: A notice reads: the company has found a way to play the second scene that is funnier and truer at once, and it has done it by removing everything the text says about the storm. What is the critic setting the production against?

The original production, since a revival is properly measured against what the play has previously been made to mean
options.misconception: supplies a comparison the notice never makes, and the text is the thing the notice is holding the production to

options.text: The audience's enjoyment, since a scene that is funnier is better and the loss of the storm is a fair price
options.misconception: substitutes pleasure for fidelity, and the notice reports the gain and the loss together

options.text: The genre, since a play of this kind is not expected to be storm-bound and the critic is defending a convention
options.misconception: makes the critic a defender of a convention, and the notice has praised the departure rather than complained of it

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An interpretation and the evidence for it
questions.learningObjective: say what counts as evidence for an interpretation of a production
questions.stem: Someone claims of an invented production that it plays the husband as the play's author, and offers two supports: that he is the only character who quotes the play's own family in his speeches, and that the production has lit every scene in which he is absent from above, through a skylight, so the house is a room he is always looking into. What does this claim need in order to be an interpretation rather than an impression?

options.text: That the two supports point the same way, since an interpretation is a reading of a pattern and two unrelated observations make a pair rather than a case
That the director has confirmed the reading, since an interpretation is a claim about intention and only the maker can say what was intended
options.misconception: makes a critic dependent on a statement of intent, which the practice of criticism does not require

options.text: That no other character quotes the family, since the claim is comparative and cannot stand unless the comparison is complete
options.misconception: adds a requirement of exhaustive evidence, when an interpretation needs a pattern and not a census

options.text: That the skylight work was intended, since a lighting effect that was found rather than planned cannot support a claim about meaning
options.misconception: requires intention for every observation, and what a production does is evidence whatever anybody meant by it

questions.explanation: An interpretation is an argument about a pattern, and the two supports have to be instances of the same pattern rather than two things that happen to be notable. Quoting the family establishes that a character is related to the text of the play in a way nobody else is, and the skylight establishes that the house is positioned as something he observes from outside; those are one claim about authorship seen twice, and together they are strong. If one of them were a joke that landed or a lighting choice made for a different reason, the claim would be an impression with a decoration on it. That is the first option, and the distinction between a pair and a case is the whole of it. The second makes criticism dependent on a statement of intent. The third demands exhaustive evidence rather than a pattern. The fourth requires intention for every observation, when what a production does is evidence whatever anybody meant.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two supports are two instances of one claim or two separate remarks.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Documentary theatre and its question
questions.learningObjective: say what question a documentary performance raises
questions.stem: An invented documentary theatre piece is built from a single document: a transcript of a public inquiry, in which each witness is described by a number and each answer is given twice, once as recorded and once as the same sentence delivered to a group of schoolchildren a month later. The company plays both versions of every answer. What question does the piece raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: What changes in an account between one room and another, and the piece treats it as a question it has arranged rather than answered, since the two deliveries are the same length and the same words
Who was telling the truth, and the piece settles it, since a witness who has said the same thing twice has been consistent and consistency is truth
options.misconception: equates consistency with accuracy, and the piece has built its method on the difference between saying and meaning

options.text: Why an inquiry was held, and the piece leaves it open, since the transcript does not say who called it and the company has not said either
options.misconception: seeks an omission as the piece's question, when the piece's method is built on what the record does contain

options.text: No question at all, since a documentary piece only reproduces material and a reproduction makes no argument
options.misconception: denies that a method is an argument, when playing each answer twice is itself a claim about the record

questions.explanation: The piece's method is the argument, and the method is to put the same words in two rooms. A witness who says exactly the same thing to a commission and to a class of schoolchildren has not varied their account, so the difference the audience can register is entirely in the room, and the piece makes that difference the thing it asks about without supplying an explanation for it. Nothing in the record distinguishes the two deliveries, so the question is about what an account is doing rather than about what happened, and the piece's refusal to settle it is deliberate: it has doubled the evidence rather than chosen between it. That is the first option, and the last clause is the design that holds the question open. The second confuses consistency with accuracy, which is precisely the substitution the piece is built to expose. The third treats a missing fact as the question. The fourth denies that a method can argue, and playing each answer twice is a claim about the record.
questions.hint: Ask what the two deliveries share, and what the piece is therefore asking about.

questions.topic: What an opening signals
questions.learningObjective: say what an opening tells an audience about the run to follow
questions.stem: A production opens with ninety seconds of the company working in silence on a set that is plainly going to be struck at the interval, and the first line of the play is spoken by somebody carrying a box. What question does the opening raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: Whether what the audience is watching is the play, and the opening treats it as a question it has decided to let the play answer, since the work goes on being done and is not commented on
Why the set is struck at the interval, and the opening treats it as settled, since a director who will strike a set has a reason the audience is not being given
options.misconception: supplies a production motive the opening has not asserted, and the interval is a fact about schedule

options.text: Whether the company is working to music or in true silence, and the opening treats it as a question left to the ear
options.misconception: seeks a technical fact, which is a matter of the sound design and not what an opening is doing

options.text: No question at all, since an opening that shows work is a statement about labour and statements require no answering
options.misconception: denies that a prelude can ask anything, when showing work in front of an audience is itself a question

That is the first option, and the last clause is what makes it a question rather than a statement. The second supplies a motive the opening never asserts. The third seeks a technical fact. The fourth denies that a prelude can ask anything, which is the premise of the whole device.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience is left having to decide, and whether the play decides it for them.

questions.topic: What an immersive piece asks of an audience
questions.learningObjective: say what participation in an immersive piece requires
questions.stem: An invented immersive piece seats its audience in the room the play is about, gives some of them tasks to carry out, and never tells them which of them are performers. What question does the piece raise, and how does it treat it?

Who the performers are, and the piece settles it, since an audience that has been given tasks has been told which of them are not playing themselves

options.text: Whether the audience is capable of the tasks, and the piece treats it as settled, since a piece that cannot be done is not a piece that is hard

The second believes a task discloses a role, and a task is the ordinary way of concealing one. The third shifts the question to competence. The fourth explains lineage and not argument.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true for the question to be settled, and what that would cost the piece.

questions.topic: An ensemble against a star-led evening
questions.learningObjective: weigh an ensemble account against a star-led one
questions.stem: Two accounts of an evening are offered. The first praises a production in which every part was well played and the effect was a crowd behaving like a crowd. The second praises a production in which one performance was so exact that it reorganised how the rest of the company played. Which account better supports the claim that the second is the more transferable achievement?

options.text: The second, since a performance that changes how the company around it plays leaves something a different cast could not have got from it, whereas a well-played evening is reproducible
The first, since an ensemble is the harder thing to achieve and therefore the achievement that other companies can learn from
options.misconception: makes difficulty the test of transferability, which is a claim about effort and not about what can be handed on

options.text: The first, since a crowd behaving like a crowd is a lesson in ensemble playing and any company can take it up
options.misconception: supplies a transferable lesson the second account has not denied, and two things can both be true

options.text: Neither, since an evening cannot be transferred at all and the question asks for a comparison the accounts do not permit
options.misconception: denies transferability outright, which is the thing the question is asking about

questions.explanation: Transferability is about what the achievement consisted of, and the two evenings consisted of different things. A well-played evening is a standard applied throughout, and a company that has seen it can decide to meet the standard; the achievement is repeatable by construction, which is its strength and also the reason it leaves nothing particular behind. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a tradition fixes and what it costs
questions.learningObjective: explain what a settled practice gives a company and what it withholds
questions.stem: A company inherits a staging of a play that is regarded as the correct one, and is told that the entrance must be made at that pace because the entrance has always been made at that pace. Explain what this arrangement gives the company, what it costs them, and what a reader of the production has to be able to do to tell the two apart.

answer.exemplar: The arrangement gives the company a solved problem, and the problem was real. An entrance made at a settled pace because of a settled difficulty, in a building with a particular sightline, is a piece of knowledge that would otherwise have to be rediscovered at the cost of somebody else's evening, and inheriting it is the ordinary and defensible use of a tradition. What it costs them is the thing the question is really about, and it is not freedom in general but a specific narrowing: a company playing inside a fixed entrance can no longer use the entrance to say anything, because every property of it has already been spent on the effect it was invented to produce, and a departure from it will be read as an error before it is read as an idea. So the cost is not that the company is forbidden from changing the entrance but that the entrance is now the one place in the production where an audience has stopped attending, and attention spent on looking is attention not available for anything else. A reader of the production has to keep two things apart: whether a moment is effective and whether it is inherited. A tradition makes the second easy to overlook precisely because the first is usually true, and a critic who reports only that an entrance was beautifully made has reported the tradition's own claim on itself. The strong explanation will name what the arrangement solves, name the specific narrowing rather than a general loss of freedom, and then state the double judgement a reader has to make. A weak answer will present the two as a simple opposition between freedom and discipline and leave it there, which is a frame the evidence in the question is designed to complicate.

questions.explanation: An explanation of an institutional arrangement has to do three things and this kind of item fails when it does the first only. It must say what the arrangement gives, and the answer is a real gain rather than a neutral acceptance, because a settled practice is stored knowledge and rediscovering it is expensive. It must say what it costs in specific terms, since a general complaint about constraint is the standard move and the question has supplied a much better one, which is that an inherited device has already been spent on its own effect. And it must state what a reader has to do differently, because the question asks for that and an answer that ends on the company's situation has not finished. The trap is treating tradition and innovation as opposites, when the difficulty is that a tradition works well enough to be invisible while it is working.
questions.hint: Ask what the entrance has already been used for, and what can no longer be asked of it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The problem of documenting a performance
questions.learningObjective: explain what cannot be recovered from a record of a performance
questions.stem: A theatre keeps a recording of every production it has staged and a copy of every text, and it has found that the recordings are the archive nobody can use. Explain what a recording of a performance cannot carry, and why having the text as well does not repair it.

answer.exemplar: A recording carries what happened to have been sounded and, from a fixed point, what could be seen, and a great deal of what makes a performance falls outside both. It does not carry why a pause was held, because a pause has no sound and only a duration, and a duration on a recording is indistinguishable from any other duration of the same length. It does not carry what the company believed about the evening, and that belief is often the most consequential thing in the room. It does not carry the audience, or rather it carries the audience as a source, which means it carries one evening's noise and the ears that produced it and not the response of any person in the room. And it does not carry the conditions, which are fixed by the accident of the record: the third night, the stalls, a company partway through a run. The text does not repair any of this, and the reason is worth stating precisely, because the obvious response is that the words are safe in the text and can be matched to the sound. But a text fixes words and not the uses of them, so the recording and the text can be aligned and the alignment still leaves the same four things missing, and it can even make them look more securely present, since a reader with a script in hand will confidently supply the intention that the recording cannot give. What the archive does have is one thing, and it is not nothing: it fixes that something happened on that night, and that is a floor for later accounts rather than a substitute for them. The strong explanation will name the four kinds of thing the recording cannot carry, will say specifically why the text cannot supply them, and will end by saying what the archive is nevertheless good for. A weak answer will list generalities about ephemerality, which is a mood rather than an analysis of a record.

questions.explanation: An explanation about documentation has to specify the losses and not gesture at them, and the specific losses here are the whole content of the answer. It must then deal with the text, because a reader will reach for the obvious repair and the question asks why it fails, and the reason is a precise one about what a printed text fixes and does not fix. And it must end by saying what the archive is good for, since an explanation that ends on loss has described a limitation and not told a theatre what to keep. The trap is the general complaint about performance being ephemeral, which sounds right and names nothing that could be acted on.
questions.hint: Ask what a pause sounds like on a recording, and what a printed page can be made to tell you about why.

questions.topic: What an ensemble evening makes and a star evening does not
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between an ensemble achievement and a star-led one
questions.stem: A notice praises one production for a performance that reorganised the company around it, and a second notice praises a production in which nothing the lead did could have been done by anybody else and the rest of the company was excellent. Explain what each evening makes, and what a reader is able to say about the work of the company as a company in each case.

answer.exemplar: The two evenings distribute the work differently, and the difference shows up in what a notice can report about the company. In the first, the lead's performance is described as reorganising, and the verb is the evidence: something was altered for everybody else, so the lead's work is inseparable from the company's and the notice cannot assign a share to the ensemble because the ensemble is where the effect landed. In the second, the lead's work is described as irreducible, which means it is separable by definition, and the remainder can then be described as excellent in its own right. So a reader can say considerably more about the second evening as a company than about the first, which is the opposite of what the first evening is usually credited for. That is worth stating plainly, because the accepted account treats the star evening as the smaller achievement and the ensemble evening as the larger one, and on the question of what can be said about a company the ordering reverses. What the first evening makes is a single indivisible event that no one could repeat and no one could inherit; what the second makes is two separable achievements, one of which belongs to the company and can be assessed, learned from, and criticised as such. The strong explanation will describe the redistribution of work in each, will say why the notice's verbs are the clue, and will then draw the uncomfortable conclusion about which evening tells a reader more about a company. A weak answer will rank the two by admiration and will treat the ensemble evening as automatically the greater, which is exactly the view the evidence in the question undercuts.

questions.explanation: An explanation comparing two achievements has to be organised on what can be said about each, and the temptation is to organise it on which one was better, which is a judgement the question has supplied enough to complicate. It must take the notices' own verbs as the evidence, since reorganising and irreducible are doing all the work in the two sentences. It must then state the conclusion that follows, which is that the evening that sounds more impressive tells a reader less about a company as a company, and that is a genuinely awkward result which an answer has to follow rather than smooth over. An answer that ends on admiration has substituted its own preference for the analysis it was asked for.
questions.hint: Ask whether the lead's work in each evening could be assigned to the company or only to the person.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim defeated by its own economics
questions.learningObjective: explain how a theatre's own arithmetic contradicts a claim about its practice
questions.stem: A theatre describes itself as a home for the classics, on the grounds that it has staged ninety plays in two hundred years, none of them written in the last twenty. The same theatre has staged three new plays in the last five. Explain what the arithmetic shows, and why the ninety is not the evidence the theatre thinks it is.

answer.exemplar: The ninety is a count of survival and the theatre is presenting it as a count of practice, and those are different quantities. Ninety productions over two centuries is what accumulates when a repertory is built on work that does not have to be replaced, and it is the wrong number to argue from because it says almost nothing about what the theatre is doing now: a single long run of one classic repeated every few years would produce a substantial total, and a repertory that mounted a dozen new classics a year would produce a smaller one. The three new plays in five years is the number that describes the present, and it points the other way, since three in five years is a rate of roughly a play a year and a company that writes at that rate with a repertory of that depth is living off the interest rather than adding to it. The claim also fails on the wording without needing the arithmetic at all, because a theatre that will not stage anything written in the last twenty years cannot be staging the classics as a practice either, since the classics are in the repertory precisely to be read against what is being written now, and a house that has stopped acquiring new work has also stopped acquiring new readers for the old. The strong explanation will separate the count of survival from the count of practice, will use the rate in the present to make the point rather than the total, and will note that the two numbers are compatible with each other, which is why the claim is not simply false but resting on the wrong figure. A weak answer will say the theatre is merely old, which is a description rather than an argument, or will treat the three new plays as evidence of hypocrisy, which assumes the theatre was not doing what it said in the years when it staged nothing new either.

questions.explanation: An explanation that turns a theatre's own figures against its claim has to do three things and the middle one is the one answers skip. It must say what the ninety counts, which is survival across a long period rather than activity, and that distinction is the argument. It must use the present rate, because a total over two centuries can be produced by a handful of durable titles and a rate over five years cannot, and the second number is the one that describes the theatre as a going concern. And it must be fair about the fact that the two numbers are consistent, so that the claim is not refuted as untrue but shown to rest on a figure that does not measure what it is offered as measuring. An answer that calls the theatre hypocritical has assumed that the two figures are inconsistent, and the question has deliberately made them consistent.
questions.hint: Ask what a total over two centuries could be produced by, and what a rate over five years cannot be.
